page.doc_title: Lunch 02 · Who looks after what, and how much capacity? — Interactive demo
page.title: Who looks after what, and how much capacity do you need?
page.lede: Slide from on-premises to IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and watch who owns each layer of the stack, then see what fixed and elastic capacity do during Nusantara Retail's 12.12 sale. Press ▶ Play to watch, or step through with Next and Back.
page.svgTitle: The shared responsibility model from on-premises to IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, then fixed versus elastic capacity during a December sale
page.svgDesc: Part one shows a stack of nine layers, from your data down to the physical datacenter, and a slider with four positions: on-premises, IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Each layer is labelled You, Shared or Microsoft, and the counts change as the slider moves; data, settings and identities always stay with you. Part two is a chart of one week of storefront demand in December with a spike on 12.12. A fixed server's capacity wastes money on normal days and causes an outage at the spike, a bigger server wastes even more, and elastic cloud capacity follows the demand curve.

steps.title: One server, every layer yours
steps.text: This stack shows the nine layers behind Nusantara Retail's storefront, from the customer data at the top down to the building at the bottom. Today everything runs on one server in the pantry, so every layer belongs to Nusantara: the data, the accounts, the code, the operating system, the hardware, the room and the power. The slider on the right is set to on-premises.

steps.title: Who fixes it at 2 a.m.?
steps.text: On-premises, responsibility is simple but heavy. When a disk fails at 2 a.m., Pak Budi drives in. When a security patch arrives, he schedules downtime. When the room overheats, that is his problem too. All nine layers are Nusantara's, and so is the capital cost of buying the hardware and replacing it every few years.

set.t-cap1: Patching, spare parts, power and cooling:
set.t-cap2: all handled by Nusantara's own team

steps.title: Slide to IaaS
steps.text: Move the slider to infrastructure as a service. Nusantara now rents virtual machines in Azure. Microsoft takes over the physical hosts, the network hardware and the datacenter, including power, cooling and guards. The operating system is still Nusantara's to patch, harden and back up, together with everything above it. Lift and shift is quick, but the daily chores remain.

set.t-ex2: you still patch the operating system
set.t-cap1: Green rows: Microsoft looks after them

steps.title: Slide to PaaS
steps.text: Platform as a service: Dewi deploys code to App Service, and the data lives in Azure SQL Database. Microsoft now patches the operating system and runs the platform. Applications and network controls become shared: Microsoft secures the platform, while Nusantara still writes secure code, decides who can reach the app and keeps its secrets safe.

set.t-ex1: e.g. App Service, Azure SQL Database
set.t-ex2: you bring the code, data and settings
set.t-cap1: Amber outline: shared, both sides have work
set.t-cap2: Green rows: Microsoft looks after them

steps.title: Slide to SaaS
steps.text: Software as a service is a finished application, such as Microsoft 365 for e-mail or an online payroll service. Microsoft now builds and runs the application itself and everything beneath it, including the network controls. Nusantara still configures the app's options, decides who may use it and looks after its own laptops and phones.

set.t-ex2: you configure it and decide who uses it

steps.title: Four layers never move
steps.text: The top four layers never change owner, whatever the model: your data, your settings, your identities and access, and your own laptops and phones. Imagine a store manager's account without MFA is phished, and the attacker exports customer data from a SaaS app. Microsoft ran its part perfectly; the gap was in Nusantara's part. The cloud shares the work, never the accountability for data and access.

steps.title: Now the capacity question
steps.text: Second question: how much capacity do you need? This chart shows a week of storefront traffic in December. The blue line is customer demand: daily ups and downs, then a huge spike on 12.12, the biggest online sale of the year. The flat line is the pantry server's capacity. On-premises, capacity is what you bought, and it stays that size.

steps.title: Most days: paying for idle
steps.text: On normal days, demand stays well below the server's capacity. The shaded band is capacity Nusantara paid for up front but did not use. That money was spent as capital expenditure, years in advance. Someone still powers, cools and patches the server every day, whether ten customers visit or ten thousand.

set.t-chart: Idle capacity is CapEx you paid for and did not use

steps.title: 12.12: demand beats capacity
steps.text: Then 12.12 arrives. Demand shoots above the line, first at the midnight flash sale and again at midday. Requests beyond capacity queue up and time out, pages crawl and checkout fails. This is the outage zone: lost sales on the most important day of the year, and frustrated customers who might not come back. One server cannot stretch.

set.t-chart: Above the line, customers see errors instead of a checkout

steps.title: Buy for the peak instead?
steps.text: The classic answer is to buy a server big enough for 12.12. The spike now fits, but look at the rest of the week, and the rest of the year: the idle band becomes enormous. The purchase takes weeks, it is still one box, and if next year's sale is bigger you are back where you started. Scaling up a fixed box trades outages for waste.

set.t-chart: Bought for the peak: no outage, but idle almost all year

steps.title: Elastic capacity follows demand
steps.text: In the cloud, capacity can follow demand. Autoscale adds web instances as traffic climbs before the sale and removes them afterwards, so the stepped green line stays just above the blue one. Nusantara pays for what it uses, hour by hour: operational expenditure that rises and falls with the business. That is elasticity, built on horizontal scaling.

set.t-chart: Elastic: pay for the capacity you need, when you need it

steps.title: Your turn: make the business case
steps.text: Recap. Each step from on-premises to IaaS, PaaS and SaaS hands more layers to Microsoft, but data, settings and identities always stay yours. Fixed capacity means paying for idle hardware or failing at the peak. Elastic capacity follows demand and turns a big up-front purchase into a monthly bill that tracks the business.
